Scientific Machine Learning:
Embedding Physical Knowledge into Neural Networks

In many scientific and engineering problems, purely data-driven learning is insufficient. Physical systems are governed by underlying structure: conservation laws, symmetries, boundary conditions, causality. A network that does not know about this structure must rediscover it from data, and it will only ever rediscover it approximately. Incorporating the structure directly improves data efficiency, generalization and physical consistency. This notebook is a systematic catalogue of how that is done — first the general choice between penalizing a violation and making it impossible, then the standard constraints one at a time, ending with the two symmetry requirements that are easiest to confuse with each other.

Everything in this notebook runs in plain PyTorch on ordinary supervised data. Nothing in this notebook solves a differential equation or differentiates a network output — each experiment fits a network to samples and then measures whether the constraint holds. The point is always the same: compare a network with the constraint built in against the same network without it, and read off what the constraint bought.


Learning Objectives¶

After studying this notebook, you should be able to

  • explain why purely data-driven learning is often insufficient for physical systems, and what is gained by building known structure into the network;
  • distinguish a soft constraint, imposed as a penalty in the loss, from a hard constraint, imposed by the architecture, and state precisely what each does and does not guarantee;
  • decide between the two from the certainty of the prior knowledge, the cost of a violation, and the tractability of an architectural encoding;
  • enforce positivity, negativity and monotonicity exactly by transforming the raw network output, and write the corresponding penalty when no exact encoding is available;
  • write boundary and initial conditions as residual penalties, and say why the resulting weights are hard to balance and why a boundary error is not a local error;
  • impose the same conditions exactly instead, by the masking parameterization $\hat{v} = g + s\,v$, and construct a masking function for a given domain;
  • enforce a global integral constraint by an additive shift, and positivity together with normalization by the continuous softmax;
  • define equivariance $f(Tq) = T f(q)$ with a transformation operator acting on both input and output, and verify that the symmetrized network $\tilde{f}(q) = \tfrac12\bigl[f(q) + R\,f(Rq)\bigr]$ satisfies it exactly;
  • define invariance $f(Tq) = f(q)$, and say when each of the two is the right requirement;
  • compare the three standard routes to a symmetry — structured layers, averaging over the group, and data augmentation — in terms of guarantee and cost;
  • implement each of these constructions in a few lines of PyTorch, and measure what the constraint bought: how far an unconstrained network drifts outside the admissible set, and how much accuracy the constrained one gave up in exchange.

Summary




1. Hard and Soft Constraints¶

Constraints on the output of a network arise from many sources: physical laws, mathematical requirements, conservation principles, symmetry properties. Whatever the origin, one question comes first — how strongly must the constraint hold? The answer divides every technique in this notebook into two families.


It helps to think of the question in two parts: what the prior knowledge is, and at what level it is enforced. When the knowledge is exact and certain — a boundary value that is prescribed, a total mass that is fixed — hard enforcement is appropriate. When it is approximate, uncertain, or too intricate to encode in the architecture, soft enforcement is the flexible alternative. The choice is therefore not a matter of implementation convenience. It records how much we trust the constraint and how much a violation would cost.

Setup

NumPy, Matplotlib and PyTorch.

In [ ]:
%matplotlib inline
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from matplotlib import pyplot as plt

1.1. Soft Constraints¶

1.1.1. The Penalty Term¶

A soft constraint enters through the loss. Instead of forcing the network to satisfy a requirement, we add a term that grows whenever the requirement is violated, and let training push it down along with everything else.


If the output is to satisfy some requirement $\mathcal{C}$, the loss becomes


$$ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{data}}(\theta) + \lambda \, \mathcal{R}(\theta) $$


where $\mathcal{R}(\theta) \geq 0$ measures the degree of violation and $\lambda > 0$ sets how strongly it is enforced. The penalty is almost always written so that it is zero on the feasible set and smooth elsewhere, because a term that is merely an indicator of infeasibility carries no gradient and teaches the optimizer nothing.

1.1.2. What a Penalty Does and Does Not Guarantee¶

The appeal of this route is its generality: any differentiable measure of violation can be used, and nothing about the architecture has to change.


The limitation is equally plain. Minimizing $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{data}} + \lambda\mathcal{R}$ trades one term against the other, so at the minimum $\mathcal{R}$ is small but not zero. The constraint is satisfied approximately, and the residual violation depends on $\lambda$, on the optimizer, and on how much the data term resists. Raising $\lambda$ shrinks the violation but stiffens the optimization problem, and in the limit $\lambda \to \infty$ the loss surface becomes ill-conditioned and training slows down or stalls. There is no value of $\lambda$ at which the constraint becomes exact.


1.2. Hard Constraints¶

A hard constraint is enforced through the architecture, so that the output satisfies it exactly for every value of the parameters $\theta$ — at initialization, during training, and at inference. Rather than penalizing a violating output, the network is redesigned so that producing one is structurally impossible. There are two standard mechanisms.

1.2.1. Output Parameterization¶

The raw output $v(x)$ is passed through a fixed transformation that lands in the constraint-satisfying set. If the output must be non-negative,


$$ \hat{v}(x) = \exp\!\bigl(v(x)\bigr) $$


is non-negative whatever $v$ does. The transformation is part of the model, so gradients flow through it and the network learns in the transformed coordinates.

1.2.2. Projection¶

A correction is applied after the raw output is computed, mapping it onto the constraint-satisfying set. If the output must have zero mean, $\int_\Omega \hat{v}(x)\,dx = 0$, subtract the mean of the raw output:


$$ \hat{v}(x) = v(x) - \frac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_\Omega v(y)\,dy $$


This guarantees $\int_\Omega \hat{v}(x)\,dx = 0$ exactly, whatever $v$ produces.


The advantage of both mechanisms is exact satisfaction, everywhere and always. Two costs come with it. Not every constraint has a simple architectural encoding — that is the main limitation. And the transformation changes the shape of the loss surface, so a parameterization that is mathematically correct can still be numerically awkward; the exponential of Section 1.2.1 is an example, since it can produce very large values before training has settled.


1.3. Choosing Between Them¶

1.3.1. Three Deciding Factors¶

Certainty of the prior knowledge. If the constraint is exact and known with certainty — a Dirichlet boundary condition, a conservation law — hard enforcement is appropriate. If it is approximate, domain-dependent, or derived from uncertain physical assumptions, soft enforcement is more robust, because a hard encoding of a slightly wrong constraint is a wrong model that cannot be corrected by data.


Cost of violation. In safety-critical or physically interpretable settings, even a small violation may be unacceptable: a negative predicted density is not a small error but a meaningless one. Hard enforcement removes the risk entirely. In exploratory or data-rich settings, approximate satisfaction is often sufficient.


Architectural tractability. Not every constraint admits a clean hard encoding. Nonlinear invariants, inequality constraints coupling several outputs, or conditions that depend on the input in a complicated way may be difficult or impossible to impose exactly. Then soft enforcement is the only practical option.

1.3.2. Combining the Two¶

The two are not exclusive, and in practice they are usually combined: hard constraints wherever an exact encoding is available, soft constraints for the remainder. This keeps the flexibility of penalty-based training while guaranteeing the structural requirements that matter most.


There is a second benefit worth noting. Every constraint moved from the loss into the architecture is one penalty weight $\lambda$ that no longer has to be tuned, and one competing term removed from the objective. Hard constraints therefore tend to make the remaining optimization problem easier, not merely more correct.


soft constraint hard constraint
imposed by a penalty term in the loss the architecture
satisfaction approximate exact, for every $\theta$
tuning requires a weight $\lambda$ none
applicability any differentiable measure of violation only constraints with a known encoding
failure mode residual violation; ill-conditioning as $\lambda$ grows no encoding exists, or the encoding distorts training




2. Positivity and Negativity Constraints¶

A positivity constraint requires the output to be non-negative everywhere,


$$ f(x) \geq 0 \qquad \forall x . $$


This arises naturally throughout engineering. Stress intensity factors, energy densities, material stiffnesses, absolute temperatures and probability densities are all non-negative by definition, and a prediction that violates the bound is not merely inaccurate — it is outside the set of physically meaningful values.


2.1. Positivity¶

2.1.1. Output Transformation¶

Pass the raw network output $v(x)$ through a strictly positive function:


$$ \hat{f}(x) = \exp\bigl(v(x)\bigr) $$


or the softplus variant


$$ \hat{f}(x) = \log\bigl(1 + \exp(v(x))\bigr) . $$


Both are positive for every real $v$, so the constraint holds by construction.


The two differ in how they behave away from the origin. The exponential grows without bound and can produce enormous values early in training, when $v$ is unconstrained; softplus is linear for large positive arguments and decays gently for large negative ones, so it is the more stable choice in practice. Where the output may legitimately be exactly zero, softplus is also the better model, since it approaches zero smoothly rather than requiring $v \to -\infty$.

2.1.2. Soft Enforcement¶

If a transformation is inconvenient — for instance when the same output must also satisfy other conditions that the transformation would break — add a penalty that acts only on the negative part:


$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pos}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{j=1}^{N} \bigl[ \max\bigl(0,\, -f(x_j)\bigr) \bigr]^2 $$


The term is zero when the output is non-negative at every sampled point and grows quadratically with the size of a violation. Two limitations follow from the formula itself. It is evaluated at a finite sample $\{x_j\}$, so it says nothing about points that were never sampled; and, being a penalty, it is only approximately satisfied even there.


2.2. Negativity¶

2.2.1. Reversing the Sign¶

A negativity constraint requires the output to be non-positive,


$$ f(x) \leq 0 \qquad \forall x , $$


which arises when the quantity is bounded above by zero: a compressive stress component, a dissipation rate written as a negative quantity, a signed distance function restricted to the interior of a domain.


Everything above carries over by negating the output. The transformations become


$$ \hat{f}(x) = -\exp\bigl(v(x)\bigr) \qquad\text{or}\qquad \hat{f}(x) = -\log\bigl(1 + \exp(v(x))\bigr) , $$


and the penalty acts on the positive part instead:


$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{neg}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{j=1}^{N} \bigl[ \max\bigl(0,\, f(x_j)\bigr) \bigr]^2 . $$

2.2.2. Which Strategy to Use¶

For a sign constraint the output transformation is almost always the right choice. It is exact, it costs one elementwise function evaluation, and it needs no tuning. The penalty is worth using only when the transformation cannot be applied — typically because the output already carries another hard constraint that the transformation would destroy.

Remark (a bound that is not at zero). A constraint $f(x) \geq a$ is the same construction shifted, $\hat{f} = a + \exp(v)$, and a two-sided bound $a \leq f(x) \leq b$ is obtained from the sigmoid, $\hat{f} = a + (b - a)\,\sigma(v)$. The pattern is general: to impose a set constraint exactly, find a smooth surjection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto that set and compose it with the network.


2.3. Positivity in Practice¶

2.3.1. An Experiment¶

The target is $e^{-3x}$, which is positive everywhere. The network is trained on $[0, 1]$ and then evaluated on $[0, 2]$, so that half of the test range lies outside the training data. This is where an unconstrained network is free to do whatever its extrapolation happens to do — including going negative.

In [ ]:
x_train = np.linspace(0, 1.0, 26)              # training range
y_train = np.exp(-3*x_train)                   # the target, positive everywhere
x_test = np.linspace(0, 2.0, 201)              # test range, twice as wide

xt = torch.tensor(x_train, dtype = torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
yt = torch.tensor(y_train, dtype = torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
xa = torch.tensor(x_test, dtype = torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)

The two models differ in one line: the transformation applied to the raw output. Passing it through the identity is the unconstrained network; passing it through the softplus is the hard constraint of Section 2.1.1.

In [ ]:
# the unconstrained network: the raw output is the prediction

torch.manual_seed(0)

net_plain = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 20), nn.Tanh(),
                         nn.Linear(20, 20), nn.Tanh(),
                         nn.Linear(20, 1))

opt = torch.optim.Adam(net_plain.parameters(), lr = 0.01)

for k in range(3000):
    loss = torch.mean((net_plain(xt) - yt)**2)

    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()

loss_plain = loss.item()
y_plain = net_plain(xa).detach().numpy().ravel()

$$ \hat{f}(x) = \log\bigl(1 + \exp(v(x))\bigr) $$

In [ ]:
# the constrained network: the raw output passes through a softplus, which is always positive

torch.manual_seed(0)

net_soft = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 20), nn.Tanh(),
                        nn.Linear(20, 20), nn.Tanh(),
                        nn.Linear(20, 1))

opt = torch.optim.Adam(net_soft.parameters(), lr = 0.01)

for k in range(3000):
    z = net_soft(xt)
    pred = torch.log(1 + torch.exp(z))         # softplus

    loss = torch.mean((pred - yt)**2)

    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()

loss_soft = loss.item()
y_soft = torch.log(1 + torch.exp(net_soft(xa))).detach().numpy().ravel()
In [ ]:
print('%-18s %10s   %14s   %s' % ('', 'train loss', 'min prediction', 'negative points'))
print('%-18s %10.2e   %+14.4f   %3d / %d'
      % ('plain network', loss_plain, y_plain.min(), np.sum(y_plain < 0), len(x_test)))
print('%-18s %10.2e   %+14.4f   %3d / %d'
      % ('softplus network', loss_soft, y_soft.min(), np.sum(y_soft < 0), len(x_test)))

                   train loss   min prediction   negative points
plain network        3.23e-05          -0.0070    23 / 201
softplus network     4.83e-07          +0.0165     0 / 201
In [ ]:
plt.figure(figsize = (12, 4))

plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
plt.plot(x_test, np.exp(-3*x_test), 'k', linewidth = 2, alpha = 0.3)
plt.plot(x_test, y_plain, 'r--', linewidth = 1.5)
plt.plot(x_test, y_soft, 'b--', linewidth = 1.5)
plt.plot(x_train, y_train, 'ko', markersize = 3)
plt.plot([0, 2], [0, 0], 'k', linewidth = 0.8)
plt.legend(['exact', 'plain network', 'softplus network', 'training data'])
plt.grid(True)
plt.xlim(0.0, 2.0)
plt.xlabel('x', fontsize = 12)
plt.ylabel('f(x)', fontsize = 12)
plt.title('the whole range', fontsize = 12)

plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
plt.plot(x_test, np.exp(-3*x_test), 'k', linewidth = 2, alpha = 0.3)
plt.plot(x_test, y_plain, 'r--', linewidth = 1.5)
plt.plot(x_test, y_soft, 'b--', linewidth = 1.5)
plt.plot([1.0, 2], [0, 0], 'k', linewidth = 0.8)
plt.grid(True)
plt.xlim(1.0, 2.0)
plt.ylim(-0.015, 0.06)
plt.xlabel('x', fontsize = 12)
plt.title('the extrapolation range, magnified')

plt.show()

Both networks fit the training range. Beyond it the unconstrained one crosses zero and stays below it, while the constrained one cannot: the softplus has no negative values in its range, so no choice of parameters and no behaviour of the extrapolation can produce one. Note also that the training loss of the constrained model is not worse — the constraint has cost nothing here, because the target satisfied it in the first place.




3. Monotonicity Constraints¶

A monotonicity constraint requires the output to change consistently in one direction as the input increases. Monotone increasing means


$$ x_1 \leq x_2 \implies f(x_1) \leq f(x_2) , $$


as for the deflection of a beam under a growing load; monotone decreasing means


$$ x_1 \leq x_2 \implies f(x_1) \geq f(x_2) , $$


as for the fatigue life of a material against the amplitude of the applied stress.


The two cases are not separate problems. A monotone decreasing function is $f(x) = -h(x)$ with $h$ monotone increasing, so every strategy in this chapter is described for the increasing case and the decreasing case follows by negation.


3.1. Monotone Increasing¶

3.1.1. Non-negative Derivative¶

Monotonicity is a statement about the derivative,


$$ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \geq 0 , $$


so one exact route is to model the derivative rather than the function, force it to be non-negative by the transformation of Chapter 2, and integrate:


$$ f(x) = f(x_0) + \int_{x_0}^{x} \exp\bigl(g(t)\bigr)\,dt $$


where $g$ is an unconstrained network. Since $\exp(g(t)) > 0$ everywhere, the integral is strictly increasing in $x$, for any $g$ and any parameters.


This gives the strongest guarantee and leaves $g$ completely free, so no expressive power is lost. Its cost is the integral, which must be evaluated numerically at every forward pass, and the constant $f(x_0)$, which becomes an additional learnable parameter.


The two cases are drawn in the figure. What the constraint asks for is visible in the tangent at every point: it may never tip the other way.


Monotone increasing (left) and monotone decreasing (right). The dashed line is the tangent at a point: for an increasing function its slope is never negative, for a decreasing one never positive. A beam deflects more as the load grows; the fatigue life of a material falls as the stress amplitude grows.

3.1.2. Monotone Architecture¶

Constrain every weight in the network to be non-negative — in practice by storing $w$ and using $\exp(w)$ or $\mathrm{softplus}(w)$ — and use only non-decreasing activations such as ReLU or the sigmoid. A composition of non-decreasing functions is non-decreasing, so the network is monotone in its input by construction, with no integral to evaluate.


The price is expressive power. Non-negative weights mean the network can never subtract one feature from another, and such a network cannot represent functions that are monotone overall but built from competing internal terms. It is the simplest construction and the most restrictive.

3.1.3. Soft Enforcement¶

Sample pairs $x_1^i \leq x_2^i$ and penalize the violations:


$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mono}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \bigl[ \max\bigl(0,\, f(x_1^i) - f(x_2^i)\bigr) \bigr]^2 $$


Zero when monotonicity holds at the sampled pairs, quadratic in the size of a violation elsewhere. As always with a penalty, the guarantee extends only to what was sampled, and only approximately.


3.2. Monotone Decreasing¶

3.2.1. Reversing the Sign¶

The same three strategies apply with the sign reversed. The integral construction becomes


$$ f(x) = f(x_0) - \int_{x_0}^{x} \exp\bigl(g(t)\bigr)\,dt , $$


the architectural route constrains all weights to be non-positive — or, equivalently and more simply, applies the monotone increasing architecture to $-f(x)$ — and the penalty reverses its argument:


$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mono}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \bigl[ \max\bigl(0,\, f(x_2^i) - f(x_1^i)\bigr) \bigr]^2 . $$

3.2.2. Which Strategy to Use¶

The non-negative derivative construction gives the strongest guarantee and keeps the network expressive; it is the default when the integral is affordable. The monotone architecture is simpler and cheaper but limits what can be represented. Soft enforcement is the easiest to add to an existing model and the only one of the three with no exact guarantee.

Remark (monotone in one input only). In several dimensions the constraint is usually required in one variable at a time — the output must increase with the load, but may do anything with the temperature. The architectural route then restricts the weights only on the path from the monotone input, and the integral route integrates only in that variable, treating the others as parameters of $g$.


3.3. Monotonicity in Practice¶

3.3.1. An Experiment¶

The data are a monotone increasing curve with noise added. The noise destroys monotonicity in the data itself — it decreases at $46$ of the $100$ intervals of the grid — so a network that fits the data closely will inherit some of that. The question is whether it has to.

In [ ]:
n = 101
x = np.linspace(0, 1, n)
dx = x[1] - x[0]

np.random.seed(0)

y_true = 1/(1 + np.exp(-10*(x - 0.5)))         # a monotone increasing curve
y_data = y_true + 0.05*np.random.randn(n)      # the noise destroys monotonicity

xt = torch.tensor(x, dtype = torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
yt = torch.tensor(y_data, dtype = torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
In [ ]:
plt.figure(figsize = (6, 4))
plt.plot(x, y_data, 'ko', markersize = 3, alpha = 0.3)
plt.xlim(0, 1)
plt.grid(True)
plt.xlabel('x', fontsize = 12)
plt.ylabel('f(x)', fontsize = 12)
plt.show()

The unconstrained network is fitted first.

In [ ]:
# the unconstrained network

torch.manual_seed(0)

net_plain = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 30), nn.Tanh(),
                         nn.Linear(30, 30), nn.Tanh(),
                         nn.Linear(30, 1))

opt = torch.optim.Adam(net_plain.parameters(), lr = 0.01)

for k in range(4000):
    loss = torch.mean((net_plain(xt) - yt)**2)

    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()

loss_plain = loss.item()
y_plain = net_plain(xt).detach().numpy().ravel()

The monotone model is the construction of Section 3.1.1, with the integral evaluated as a cumulative sum on the same grid and the starting value $f(x_0)$ learned along with the network.


$$ f(x) = f(x_0) + \int_{x_0}^{x} \exp\bigl(g(t)\bigr)\,dt , $$

In [ ]:
# the monotone network: the network gives the rate, the curve is its running integral

torch.manual_seed(0)

g = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 30), nn.Tanh(),
                 nn.Linear(30, 30), nn.Tanh(),
                 nn.Linear(30, 1))

f0 = torch.zeros(1, requires_grad = True)      # the starting value, also learned

opt = torch.optim.Adam(list(g.parameters()) + [f0], lr = 0.01)

for k in range(4000):
    rate = torch.exp(g(xt))                    # exp makes the rate positive
    f = f0 + dx*torch.cumsum(rate, 0) - dx*rate[0]

    loss = torch.mean((f - yt)**2)

    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()

loss_mono = loss.item()

rate = torch.exp(g(xt))
y_mono = (f0 + dx*torch.cumsum(rate, 0) - dx*rate[0]).detach().numpy().ravel()
In [ ]:
d_data = np.diff(y_data)                       # the step between neighbouring points
d_plain = np.diff(y_plain)
d_mono = np.diff(y_mono)

print('%-18s %10s   %16s   %s' % ('', 'train loss', 'decreasing steps', 'most negative step'))
print('%-18s %10s   %6d / %-7d   %+.2e'
      % ('the noisy data', '-', np.sum(d_data < 0), n - 1, d_data.min()))
print('%-18s %10.2e   %6d / %-7d   %+.2e'
      % ('plain network', loss_plain, np.sum(d_plain < 0), n - 1, d_plain.min()))
print('%-18s %10.2e   %6d / %-7d   %+.2e'
      % ('monotone network', loss_mono, np.sum(d_mono < 0), n - 1, d_mono.min()))

print('')
print('error against the true monotone curve')
print('   plain     %.2e' % np.mean((y_plain - y_true)**2))
print('   monotone  %.2e' % np.mean((y_mono - y_true)**2))

                   train loss   decreasing steps   most negative step
the noisy data              -       46 / 100       -1.79e-01
plain network        2.11e-03       12 / 100       -5.88e-03
monotone network     2.17e-03        0 / 100       +5.98e-04

error against the true monotone curve
   plain     5.00e-04
   monotone  4.99e-04
In [ ]:
plt.figure(figsize = (6, 4))
plt.plot(x, y_data, 'ko', markersize = 3, alpha = 0.3)
plt.plot(x, y_plain, 'r--', linewidth = 1.5)
plt.plot(x, y_mono, 'b--', linewidth = 1.5)
plt.legend(['noisy data', 'plain network', 'monotone network'])
plt.xlim([0, 1])
plt.grid(True)
plt.xlabel('x', fontsize = 12)
plt.ylabel('f(x)', fontsize = 12)
plt.show()

Read the two error figures together. The unconstrained network decreases at twelve of the hundred intervals, following the noise; the constrained one decreases nowhere, because it cannot. And the error against the true curve is the same to three digits for both. The constraint removed every violation and cost no accuracy at all — which is what one should expect whenever the prior knowledge is correct.




4. Boundary and Initial Conditions¶

For a differential equation, the solution must satisfy prescribed conditions on the boundary of the domain and, for time-dependent problems, at the initial instant. Without them the equation alone does not determine a solution, so these conditions are not decoration: they are what makes the problem well posed.


Both routes of Chapter 1 are available. The conditions can be added to the loss as residuals, which is what a physics-informed network does by default, or they can be built into the output so that they hold identically. This chapter presents the penalty first, because it is the standard arrangement and because its difficulties are what motivate the construction that follows.


4.1. Soft Enforcement¶

4.1.1. The Boundary and Initial Residuals¶

In a physics-informed setting the loss is already a sum of residuals, and the conditions simply join it as two more terms:


$$ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PDE}}(\theta) + \lambda_{b}\,\mathcal{L}_{b}(\theta) + \lambda_{0}\,\mathcal{L}_{0}(\theta) , $$


where the boundary term is the mean squared violation of $v = g$ at points sampled on $\partial\Omega$,


$$ \mathcal{L}_{b}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N_{b}} \sum_{j=1}^{N_{b}} \bigl( \hat{v}(x_j) - g(x_j) \bigr)^{2} , \qquad x_j \in \partial\Omega , $$


and the initial term is the same thing at $t = 0$,


$$ \mathcal{L}_{0}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N_{0}} \sum_{j=1}^{N_{0}} \bigl( \hat{v}(x_j, 0) - v_0(x_j) \bigr)^{2} . $$


Nothing about the network changes. The conditions are sampled like any other data, and the optimizer is asked to reconcile them with the equation residual.

4.1.2. What the Penalty Costs¶

This arrangement works, and for a domain whose geometry admits no convenient parameterization it is the only practical option. But it has four costs that are worth naming, because each of them disappears under the construction of Section 4.2.


The conditions compete with the equation. At the minimum of a weighted sum, no term is zero. The network settles at a compromise in which the boundary is slightly wrong and the equation is slightly wrong, and the balance point is set by $\lambda_b$ and $\lambda_0$ rather than by the physics.


The weights are hard to choose. The three terms have different units and different typical magnitudes, and the right ratio changes during training. Too small a $\lambda_b$ and the network ignores the boundary; too large and the boundary term dominates the early gradients, the network fits the edges of the domain first, and the interior is learned slowly against a stiff objective.


A boundary error is not a local error. For an elliptic problem the solution at every interior point depends on the whole boundary, so a small violation at the edge is not confined to the edge — it propagates inward and shifts the entire field. The same is true in time: an error in the initial condition is carried along the whole trajectory.


Only sampled points are constrained. The penalty says nothing about the parts of the boundary that were not sampled, which matters most exactly where the geometry is complicated and the sampling is thin.


The conditions of a well-posed problem are, however, known exactly — they are prescribed, not inferred. By the criteria of Section 1.3.1 they are the clearest candidates in this notebook for hard enforcement, and the rest of the chapter shows how.


4.2. Boundary Conditions¶

4.2.1. The Masking Construction¶

Suppose the output must satisfy $v(x) = g(x)$ on the boundary $\partial\Omega$. Construct the network output as


$$ \hat{v}(x) = g(x) + s(x)\,v(x) $$


where $v$ is the raw network output and $s$ is a masking function with


$$ s(x) = 0 \ \text{ on } \partial\Omega , \qquad s(x) > 0 \ \text{ inside } \Omega . $$


On the boundary the second term vanishes and $\hat{v} = g$ exactly, whatever the network produces. Inside the domain $s > 0$, so the network retains full freedom, merely rescaled.


Compare this with Section 4.1. The boundary condition is now satisfied at initialization, so training never spends capacity learning it; it remains satisfied at every later iteration, so it cannot be traded against the equation residual; it holds at every boundary point, not only the sampled ones; and the weight $\lambda_b$ has disappeared from the objective altogether. The loss is left with the equation residual alone.

4.2.2. Choosing a Masking Function¶

The masking function depends on the geometry of the domain. For the unit interval $\Omega = (0, 1)$ the simplest choice is


$$ s(x) = x(1 - x) , $$


which vanishes at both endpoints and is positive in between. With homogeneous conditions $g = 0$ the parameterization reduces to


$$ \hat{v}(x) = x(1 - x)\,v(x) . $$


For a product domain the masks multiply. On the unit square $\Omega = (0,1)^2$,


$$ s(x_1, x_2) = x_1(1 - x_1)\,x_2(1 - x_2) , $$


which vanishes on all four edges by construction.

Remark (what the mask costs). A mask that decays quickly near the boundary forces $\hat{v}$ to be small there, so the network must produce large values of $v$ to represent a solution with a steep boundary layer. The construction is exact for any admissible $s$, but the conditioning of training is not indifferent to the choice; masks that vanish linearly, as above, are generally better behaved than higher-order ones. For a domain with no simple algebraic description, an approximate distance function to $\partial\Omega$ serves the same purpose.


4.3. Initial Conditions¶

4.3.1. Temporal Masking¶

For a time-dependent problem the output must satisfy $v(x, 0) = v_0(x)$. The same idea applies with a mask in time:


$$ \hat{v}(x, t) = v_0(x) + \tau(t)\,v(x, t) $$


where $\tau(0) = 0$ and $\tau(t) > 0$ for $t > 0$. At $t = 0$ the second term vanishes and $\hat{v}(x, 0) = v_0(x)$ exactly.


The simplest choice is $\tau(t) = t$. Another common one is


$$ \tau(t) = 1 - e^{-\alpha t} , \qquad \alpha > 0 , $$


which also vanishes at $t = 0$ but saturates instead of growing, so the network contribution is not scaled up at late times. The parameter $\alpha$ controls how quickly the network is switched on relative to the initial condition, and is worth choosing on the time scale of the problem.

4.3.2. What the Parameterization Achieves¶

In both cases the output has been split into a constraint-carrying part — the known boundary or initial value — and a free part, the network. The network is unconstrained on the interior and for $t > 0$; the condition holds by construction where it is prescribed.


The same pattern will appear again in Chapter 5 and Chapter 6: identify what must hold exactly, build a form in which it holds identically, and let the network occupy whatever freedom is left. That is the general recipe behind every hard constraint in this notebook.


In practice the two routes of this chapter are often mixed, as Section 1.3.2 described. A Dirichlet condition on a simple part of the boundary is absorbed into the mask, while a condition on an irregular part, or a Neumann condition for which no convenient mask is at hand, is left in the loss as a residual. Each condition moved into the parameterization is one weight fewer to tune and one competing term fewer in the objective.


4.4. Masking in Practice¶

4.4.1. An Experiment¶

The target vanishes at both ends of $(0, 1)$, and the training data are drawn from the interior only: there is no sample at $x = 0$ or $x = 1$. This is the situation the masking parameterization is built for — the condition is known exactly even though nothing in the data says so.

In [ ]:
np.random.seed(0)

x_train = np.linspace(0.08, 0.92, 22)          # no sample at x = 0 or x = 1
y_train = np.sin(np.pi*x_train)*(1 + 0.3*x_train) + 0.02*np.random.randn(22)

x_test = np.linspace(0, 1, 201)
u_test = np.sin(np.pi*x_test)*(1 + 0.3*x_test) # the exact solution, zero at both ends

xt = torch.tensor(x_train, dtype = torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
yt = torch.tensor(y_train, dtype = torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
xa = torch.tensor(x_test, dtype = torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
In [ ]:
plt.figure(figsize = (6, 4))
plt.plot(x_train, y_train, 'ko', markersize = 4, alpha = 0.3)
plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 0], 'k', linewidth = 0.8)
plt.xlim([0, 1])
plt.grid(True)
plt.xlabel('x', fontsize = 12)
plt.ylabel('u(x)', fontsize = 12)
plt.show()

The mask is the simplest admissible one for this domain, $s(x) = x(1-x)$, and the boundary values are homogeneous, so the parameterization is $\hat{v} = s\,v$.

In [ ]:
# the unconstrained network

torch.manual_seed(0)

net_plain = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 20), nn.Tanh(),
                         nn.Linear(20, 20), nn.Tanh(),
                         nn.Linear(20, 1))

opt = torch.optim.Adam(net_plain.parameters(), lr = 0.01)

for k in range(3000):
    loss = torch.mean((net_plain(xt) - yt)**2)

    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()

loss_plain = loss.item()
y_plain = net_plain(xa).detach().numpy().ravel()

$$ \hat{v}(x) = x(1 - x)\,v(x) . $$

In [ ]:
# the masked network: the output is multiplied by s(x) = x(1 - x), which vanishes at both ends

torch.manual_seed(0)

net_mask = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 20), nn.Tanh(),
                        nn.Linear(20, 20), nn.Tanh(),
                        nn.Linear(20, 1))

opt = torch.optim.Adam(net_mask.parameters(), lr = 0.01)

for k in range(3000):
    pred = xt*(1 - xt)*net_mask(xt)

    loss = torch.mean((pred - yt)**2)

    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()

loss_mask = loss.item()
y_mask = (xa*(1 - xa)*net_mask(xa)).detach().numpy().ravel()
In [ ]:
print('%-16s %10s   %10s   %10s   %s' % ('', 'train loss', 'u(0)', 'u(1)', 'max error on [0,1]'))
print('%-16s %10.2e   %+.3e   %+.3e   %.2e'
      % ('plain network', loss_plain, y_plain[0], y_plain[-1], np.max(np.abs(y_plain - u_test))))
print('%-16s %10.2e   %+.3e   %+.3e   %.2e'
      % ('masked network', loss_mask, y_mask[0], y_mask[-1], np.max(np.abs(y_mask - u_test))))

                 train loss         u(0)         u(1)   max error on [0,1]
plain network      2.52e-04   +3.413e-02   +6.698e-02   6.70e-02
masked network     2.66e-04   +0.000e+00   +0.000e+00   3.09e-02
In [ ]:
plt.figure(figsize = (6, 4))
plt.plot(x_test, y_plain, 'r--', linewidth = 1.5)
plt.plot(x_test, y_mask, 'b--', linewidth = 1.5)
plt.plot(x_train, y_train, 'ko', markersize = 4, alpha = 0.3)
plt.legend(['plain network', 'masked network', 'training data'])

The masked network returns exactly zero at both ends — not approximately, and not as a result of training, but because $s$ vanishes there and the product with anything finite is zero. The unconstrained network misses at both ends, and those are the largest errors it makes anywhere: the worst part of the solution is precisely the part the prior knowledge already determined. Removing it also halves the maximum error over the whole interval.




5. Conservation Laws and Invariants¶

A conservation law requires that some quantity computed from the output remains fixed. Unlike the conditions of Chapter 4, which act pointwise, a conservation law is a single scalar condition on the output as a whole — which is what makes it awkward for a network that produces its output one point at a time, and what makes the corrections below worth knowing.


5.1. An Integral Constraint¶

5.1.1. Soft Enforcement¶

The most common form is a global integral constraint,


$$ \int_\Omega v(x)\,dx = C , $$


where $C$ is a prescribed constant such as a total mass or a total energy. The penalty is the squared violation,


$$ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{data}}(\theta) + \lambda\left(\int_\Omega \mathcal{G}_\theta(u)(x)\,dx - C\right)^{2} , $$


with $\mathcal{G}_\theta(u)$ the predicted field. The integral itself is evaluated by quadrature, so the accuracy of the constraint is limited by the accuracy of that quadrature as well as by $\lambda$.


A control volume is the physical picture behind such a constraint. Whatever crosses the boundary inwards must be balanced by what crosses it outwards, so the quantity held inside is fixed no matter how the field inside rearranges itself.


A conserved quantity as a control volume. At steady state the net flow in equals the net flow out, so the contents are fixed. The constraint is one number for the whole region, not a condition at each point — which is why it is imposed on an integral of the output rather than on the output itself.

5.1.2. Hard Enforcement by an Additive Shift¶

Because the constraint is a single scalar condition and the correction has a single degree of freedom, it can be imposed exactly by shifting the raw output by a constant:


$$ \hat{v}(x) = v(x) + \frac{C - \int_\Omega v(y)\,dy}{|\Omega|} $$


Integrating both sides over $\Omega$ gives $\int_\Omega \hat{v} = \int_\Omega v + \bigl(C - \int_\Omega v\bigr) = C$ exactly, for any $v$. This is the projection of Section 1.2.2: the raw output is mapped onto the affine set of functions with the prescribed integral, along the direction of the constants.


The shift changes the mean of the output and nothing else, so all the structure the network has learned is preserved. Its one requirement is that the integral of $v$ be available at every forward pass, which again means quadrature — here it enters the model rather than the loss.


5.2. Positivity and Normalization Together¶

5.2.1. The Continuous Softmax¶

When the conserved quantity must also be non-negative — a probability density, a concentration, a mass distribution — the additive shift of Section 5.1.2 will not do, because a shift can push values below zero. Both conditions are imposed at once by the continuous softmax:


$$ \hat{v}(x) = \frac{\exp\bigl(v(x)\bigr)}{\int_\Omega \exp\bigl(v(y)\bigr)\,dy} $$


The numerator is positive by the argument of Section 2.1.1, and dividing by the integral of the numerator makes the result integrate to one. Hence $\hat{v}(x) > 0$ everywhere and $\int_\Omega \hat{v}(x)\,dx = 1$, exactly, for any $v$.


This is the discrete softmax of a classification network with the sum replaced by an integral, and it inherits the same practical caution: the exponential should be evaluated after subtracting $\max_x v(x)$, so that the largest exponent is zero and the computation does not overflow.

Remark (normalizing to a constant other than one). For $\int_\Omega \hat{v} = C$ with $C \neq 1$, multiply the softmax by $C$. The construction does not extend as cleanly to several simultaneous integral constraints, which in general require a projection onto the intersection of the corresponding affine sets — a small linear solve rather than a closed-form correction.


5.3. Corrections in Practice¶

5.3.1. An Experiment¶

A density is learned from noisy measurements. The true field is non-negative and integrates to one, but the measurements are not: the noise carries several of them below zero in the tail, where the density is nearly exhausted. The same network is trained four times — with no constraint, with the penalty of Section 5.1.1, with the additive shift of Section 5.1.2 applied to the output at every step, and with the continuous softmax of Section 5.2.1. The last two make the integral exact by construction, so the question is what each of them does to the sign.

In [ ]:
n = 101
x = np.linspace(0, 1, n)
dx = x[1] - x[0]

np.random.seed(0)

p = np.exp(-60*(x - 0.35)**2) + 0.7*np.exp(-120*(x - 0.72)**2)


def integral(f):
    return (0.5*(f[1:] + f[:-1])*dx).sum()     # trapezoid rule, for arrays and for tensors


p = p/integral(p)                              # the true density, with integral 1

idx = np.arange(0, n, 4)                       # 26 noisy measurements
y_obs = p[idx] + 0.1*np.random.randn(len(idx))

xt = torch.tensor(x, dtype = torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
xo = xt[idx]
yo = torch.tensor(y_obs, dtype = torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)

plt.figure(figsize = (6, 4))
plt.plot(x, p, 'k', linewidth = 2, alpha = 0.2)
plt.plot(x[idx], y_obs, 'ko', markersize = 4, alpha = 0.5)
plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 0], 'k', linewidth = 0.8)
plt.xlim([0, 1])
plt.legend(['true density', 'measurements'])
plt.grid(True)
plt.xlabel('x', fontsize = 12)
plt.ylabel('v(x)', fontsize = 12)
plt.show()
In [ ]:
# no constraint: the raw output is the density

torch.manual_seed(0)

net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 30), nn.Tanh(),
                    nn.Linear(30, 30), nn.Tanh(),
                    nn.Linear(30, 1))

opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr = 0.01)

for k in range(4000):
    loss = torch.mean((net(xo) - yo)**2)

    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()

v_plain = net(xt).detach().numpy().ravel()

$$ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{data}}(\theta) + \lambda\left(\int_\Omega \mathcal{G}_\theta(u)(x)\,dx - C\right)^{2} , $$

In [ ]:
# soft: the squared violation of the integral is added to the loss

torch.manual_seed(0)

net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 30), nn.Tanh(),
                    nn.Linear(30, 30), nn.Tanh(),
                    nn.Linear(30, 1))

opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr = 0.01)

for k in range(4000):
    v = net(xt)

    loss = torch.mean((net(xo) - yo)**2) + 10.0*(integral(v) - 1)**2

    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()

v_soft = net(xt).detach().numpy().ravel()

$$ \hat{v}(x) = v(x) + \frac{C - \int_\Omega v(y)\,dy}{|\Omega|} $$

In [ ]:
# hard: the output is shifted at every step, so the integral is exact throughout training

torch.manual_seed(0)

net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 30), nn.Tanh(),
                    nn.Linear(30, 30), nn.Tanh(),
                    nn.Linear(30, 1))

opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr = 0.01)

for k in range(4000):
    v = net(xt)
    v = v + (1 - integral(v))

    loss = torch.mean((v[idx] - yo)**2)

    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()

v = net(xt)
v_shift = (v + (1 - integral(v))).detach().numpy().ravel()

$$ \hat{v}(x) = \frac{\exp\bigl(v(x)\bigr)}{\int_\Omega \exp\bigl(v(y)\bigr)\,dy} $$

In [ ]:
# hard: the continuous softmax gives the integral and the sign at once

torch.manual_seed(0)

net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 30), nn.Tanh(),
                    nn.Linear(30, 30), nn.Tanh(),
                    nn.Linear(30, 1))

opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr = 0.01)

for k in range(4000):
    e = torch.exp(net(xt))
    v = e/integral(e)

    loss = torch.mean((v[idx] - yo)**2)

    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()

e = torch.exp(net(xt))
v_softmax = (e/integral(e)).detach().numpy().ravel()
In [ ]:
print('%-22s %9s   %10s   %9s   %s' % ('', 'integral', 'min value', 'negative', 'error vs true'))

for name, v in [('plain network', v_plain), ('soft penalty', v_soft),
                ('additive shift', v_shift), ('continuous softmax', v_softmax)]:
    print('%-22s %9.5f   %+10.5f   %9d   %.4f'
          % (name, integral(v), v.min(), np.sum(v < 0), np.sqrt(np.mean((v - p)**2))))

# the two corrections applied to the same unconstrained output, for comparison

v_a = v_plain + (1 - integral(v_plain))        # additive shift
v_b = v_plain/integral(v_plain)                # rescaling

print('')
print('distance from the unconstrained output, among the corrections with the right integral')
print('   additive shift  %.5f' % np.sqrt(integral((v_a - v_plain)**2)))
print('   rescaling       %.5f' % np.sqrt(integral((v_b - v_plain)**2)))

soft penalty             1.00355     -0.06394           6   0.0881
additive shift           1.00000     -0.08955           5   0.0955
continuous softmax       1.00000     +0.00056           0   0.0997

distance from the unconstrained output, among the corrections with the right integral
   additive shift  0.03739
   rescaling       0.04986

plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
plt.plot(x, p, 'k', linewidth = 2, alpha = 0.2)
plt.plot(x[idx], y_obs, 'ko', markersize = 4, alpha = 0.5)
plt.plot(x, v_plain, 'r--', linewidth = 1.5)
plt.plot(x, v_softmax, 'b--', linewidth = 1.5)

plt.legend(['true density', 'measurements', 'plain network', 'continuous softmax'], fontsize = 10)
plt.grid(True)
