The unconstrained network misses the prescribed integral, and the penalty brings it closer but never to the exact value; what remains is the price of a finite $\lambda$. The shift and the softmax are exact to every digit printed, because in their case the integral is not something the optimizer is asked to achieve.


What separates the two is the sign. The shift subtracts one constant from the whole field, and the constant it must subtract here is positive, so the correction pushes the tail further below zero than the plain network already was. The softmax has no negative values to lose, and it satisfies both requirements at once, no further from the true density than the shift is. The last two lines confirm the claim of Section 5.1.2 along the way, that among the corrections which give the right integral the shift is the smaller one, which is exactly the point: a correction can be optimal in one norm and still be inadmissible, and when the quantity is a density the constraint to be satisfied is the pair.




6. Equivariance¶

Many networks are asked to learn mappings that respect a symmetry of the underlying physics. If the input is rotated, translated or reflected, the output should transform accordingly. Building that structure into the network improves data efficiency and guarantees consistent predictions on transformed inputs, which no amount of training on untransformed data can.


6.1. What Equivariance Means¶

6.1.1. Definition¶

Let $f$ be a network and $T$ a transformation — a rotation, a translation, a reflection. The network is equivariant with respect to $T$ when it commutes with it:


$$ f(Tq) = T\,f(q) $$


Transforming the input and then applying the network gives the same result as applying the network and then transforming the output.


Two points about the notation are worth making explicit, because they are the source of most confusion later. First, the same symbol $T$ appears on both sides but acts on different spaces: on the left it transforms the input of the network, on the right it transforms the output. Second, $T$ acts on whole functions, not on numbers. If the input is a field $q$ defined on a domain, then $Tq$ is another field, and the action of $T$ on the output is whatever the corresponding transformation of that output is — a rotation of a velocity field rotates both the positions and the vectors.

6.1.2. Examples¶

A network predicting the velocity field of a fluid should be equivariant to rotation: rotating the whole flow configuration by ninety degrees should rotate the predicted velocity field by ninety degrees.


A network predicting a temperature distribution from a heat source should be equivariant to translation: shifting the source to the right should shift the entire predicted field by the same amount.


In both cases the network that is equivariant responds correctly to a transformed input without ever having been trained on one. A network that is not equivariant may respond to the rotated configuration with a field that is not the rotation of anything it predicted before — and no inspection of its loss on the training set would reveal that.


The figure collects the transformations that occur most often. In each case the same $T$ acts on the input and on the output, which is the content of $f(Tx) = T f(x)$.


Transformations that commute with an equivariant network. Translation, rotation, reflection and permutation of labelled objects are the four that appear most often. Equivariance is the requirement that moving the input by $T$ moves the output by the same $T$.


6.2. Enforcing Equivariance¶

6.2.1. Group-Equivariant Layers¶

Build the symmetry into the layers, by constructing weight-sharing patterns that commute with the transformation. The canonical example is the convolution layer, which is equivariant to translation: the same filter is applied at every position, so shifting the input shifts the output by the same amount. Group convolutional networks extend the idea to rotations by sharing weights across rotated copies of each filter.


This gives exact equivariance at one forward pass, which is the strongest of the three routes. It requires designing the layer for the group in question, and not every group has a convenient one.

6.2.2. Output Symmetrization¶

Leave the architecture alone and average the network over the group. For a finite set of transformations $\{T_1, T_2, \ldots, T_n\}$,


$$ \tilde{f}(q) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} T_i^{-1} f(T_i q) $$


Each term transforms the input by $T_i$, applies the network, and then undoes the transformation on the output with $T_i^{-1}$. Every term is therefore a prediction expressed in the original frame, and averaging them gives a result that no longer depends on which frame was used.


The construction is exact for any $f$, needs no change to the architecture, and costs $n$ forward passes per input.

6.2.3. Data Augmentation¶

Show the network transformed versions of each training example. From a training pair $(q_i, y_i)$, generate


$$ (T q_i,\; T y_i) $$


for various $T$ — note that the label is transformed as well, since that is what equivariance asserts.


This requires no change to the architecture or to inference, and is by far the easiest route. It is also the weakest: the network is encouraged to be equivariant on the transformations and inputs it has seen, and may still be measurably inequivariant on unseen ones.


Of the three, group-equivariant layers give the strongest guarantee, data augmentation the weakest. Output symmetrization sits in between: exact and architecture-free, at the price of $n$ forward passes.


6.3. A Worked Case: the Clamped-Clamped Beam¶

6.3.1. The Reflection Operator¶

Consider a clamped-clamped beam on $x \in [-L/2,\, L/2]$, with the origin at the centre. Given a distributed load $q(x)$, the network predicts the deflection, $v = f(q)$.


The relevant transformation is the reflection about the centre of the beam. Written as an operator acting on a function,


$$ (Rq)(x) = q(-x) , $$


so $Rq$ is the load obtained by flipping the beam left to right. The same operator acts on deflections, $(Rv)(x) = v(-x)$. Reflecting twice returns the original function, so


$$ R^2 = I \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad R^{-1} = R , $$


and $\{I, R\}$ is a group with two elements.


The physics is equivariant under $R$. Flipping the load flips the deflection and does nothing else, because the beam and its supports are themselves symmetric about $x = 0$. Writing $f^{\star}$ for the exact solution operator,


$$ f^{\star}(Rq) = R\,f^{\star}(q) . $$


A network $f$ trained without any symmetry constraint does not satisfy this. Nothing in a data-fitting loss forces it to.


The figure is that statement drawn once. The top row sends a load through the network and obtains a deflection; the bottom row sends the mirrored load through the same network, and the deflection that comes out is the mirror of the first.


Equivariance of the clamped-clamped beam. Top: a load $q$ and the deflection $v = f(q)$ predicted from it. Bottom: the mirrored load $Rq$, whose deflection is the mirrored deflection $R\,f(q)$. The beam and its supports are symmetric about $x = 0$, so nothing distinguishes the two situations except the reflection itself.

6.3.2. The Symmetrized Network¶

Apply the construction of Section 6.2.2 to the group $\{I, R\}$. With $n = 2$, $T_1 = I$ and $T_2 = R$, and using $R^{-1} = R$,


$$ \tilde{f}(q) = \frac{1}{2}\Bigl[\, f(q) + R\,f(Rq) \,\Bigr] $$


Read it as three operations. Pass the load through the network. Pass the flipped load through the same network and flip the resulting deflection back. Average the two.


Written pointwise, with $v = f(q)$ and $\bar{v} = f(Rq)$,


$$ \tilde{v}(x) = \frac{1}{2}\bigl[\, v(x) + \bar{v}(-x) \,\bigr] . $$


The construction is exactly equivariant, and the verification is two lines. Using $R^2 = I$,


$$ \tilde{f}(Rq) = \frac{1}{2}\Bigl[ f(Rq) + R\,f(R^{2}q) \Bigr] = \frac{1}{2}\Bigl[ f(Rq) + R\,f(q) \Bigr] , $$


while applying $R$ to the output gives


$$ R\,\tilde{f}(q) = \frac{1}{2}\Bigl[ R\,f(q) + R^{2}f(Rq) \Bigr] = \frac{1}{2}\Bigl[ R\,f(q) + f(Rq) \Bigr] . $$


The two right-hand sides are the same, so


$$ \tilde{f}(Rq) = R\,\tilde{f}(q) $$


holds identically — for every load, and for every value of the parameters, even if the network $f$ has learned nothing about the symmetry at all. The cost is two forward passes instead of one.


The construction is easiest to read as a picture.


The two terms of the average. The upper beam carries the original load and gives $f(q)$; the lower one carries the flipped load, and its deflection is flipped back to give $R\,f(Rq)$. Both are now expressed in the same frame, so averaging them is meaningful — and the average is equivariant whatever the network has learned.

6.3.3. A Symmetric Load as a Special Case¶

Equivariance is a statement about all loads. The familiar special case follows from it in one line.


A symmetric load is one that the reflection leaves unchanged — a fixed point of $R$:


$$ Rq = q , \qquad\text{that is}\qquad q(-x) = q(x) . $$


Apply the equivariance established in Section 6.3.2 to such a load. Since $\tilde{f}(Rq) = R\,\tilde{f}(q)$ holds for every load, and $Rq = q$ for this one,


$$ R\,\tilde{f}(q) = \tilde{f}(Rq) = \tilde{f}(q) , $$


which written pointwise is


$$ \tilde{v}(-x) = \tilde{v}(x) . $$


The predicted deflection is even. This is what one expects physically — a beam that is symmetric about its centre, loaded symmetrically, deflects symmetrically — but it is worth seeing that nothing extra had to be imposed to obtain it. Symmetry of the response is a consequence of equivariance, applied to a load that happens to be a fixed point of $R$.


What the construction reduces to. For a symmetric load the two forward passes of Section 6.3.2 are calls to the network on the same input, since $Rq = q$. The symmetrized prediction


$$ \tilde{f}(q) = \frac{1}{2}\Bigl[\, f(q) + R\,f(Rq) \,\Bigr] = \frac{1}{2}\Bigl[\, f(q) + R\,f(q) \,\Bigr] $$


is therefore obtained in three steps and one forward pass:

  1. Pass the load $q$ through the network to obtain the raw deflection $v = f(q)$.
  2. Flip the output: $Rv$, that is $v(-x)$.
  3. Average the two.

$$ \tilde{v}(x) = \frac{v(x) + v(-x)}{2} $$


In words, the symmetrized prediction is the even part of the raw prediction. Whatever antisymmetric component the network produced — and an unconstrained network will produce one, since nothing in a data-fitting loss forbids it — is discarded, and $\tilde{v}(-x) = \tilde{v}(x)$ holds by construction.


6.4. Checking Equivariance Numerically¶

6.4.1. An Experiment¶

The beam of Section 6.3 is the test case. A unit point load acts at position $c$ on the beam, and the network reads $c$ and returns the deflection at the $m = 21$ interior grid points. For a point load the exact deflection is available in closed form: with $a = c + L/2$ the distance of the load from the left support and $b = L - a$,


$$ v(s) = \frac{b^{2} s^{2}\,\bigl[\,3aL - (3a + b)\,s\,\bigr]}{6\,EI\,L^{3}} \quad (s \le a) , $$


and the same expression with $a$ and $b$ exchanged and $s$ replaced by $L - s$ for $s \ge a$. It serves as the truth. The reflection $R$ sends a load at $c$ to a load at $-c$ and reverses the order of the grid values of the deflection, so the network is asked to satisfy $f(-c) = R\,f(c)$.


The symmetry is withheld from the data on purpose: every training load lies on the left half of the beam, $c \in [-0.35, -0.05]$, while the test loads lie anywhere, $c \in [-0.40, 0.40]$. Two of the routes of Section 6.2 are compared against the unconstrained network: data augmentation, and the symmetrization of Section 6.2.2 built in from the start, so that what the optimizer sees is $\tilde{f}$ rather than $f$.

In [ ]:
L = 1.0
m = 21                                         # interior grid points
x = np.linspace(-L/2, L/2, m + 2)[1:-1]        # the beam, origin at the centre

def deflection(c):                             # exact deflection for a unit point load at x = c
    a = c + L/2                                # distance of the load from the left support
    b = L - a
    s = x + L/2                                # distance of each grid point from the left support

    v = np.zeros(m)

    left = s <= a
    v[left] = b**2*s[left]**2*(3*a*L - (3*a + b)*s[left])/(6*L**3)

    r = L - s[~left]
    v[~left] = a**2*r**2*(3*b*L - (3*b + a)*r)/(6*L**3)

    return v


R = np.eye(m)[::-1].copy()                     # reflection: reverses the order of the entries

print('R is an involution                 || R R - I ||       = %.2e' % np.linalg.norm(R.dot(R) - np.eye(m)))
print('the exact operator is equivariant  || f(Rq) - R f(q) || = %.2e'
      % np.linalg.norm(deflection(-0.2) - R.dot(deflection(0.2))))
print('centre deflection %.6e   P L^3 / 192 EI = %.6e' % (deflection(0.0).max(), 1/192))

R is an involution                 || R R - I ||       = 0.00e+00
the exact operator is equivariant  || f(Rq) - R f(q) || = 4.46e-18
centre deflection 5.208333e-03   P L^3 / 192 EI = 5.208333e-03
In [ ]:
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
c_train = rng.uniform(-0.35, -0.05, 300)       # every training load sits on the left half

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
c_test = rng.uniform(-0.40, 0.40, 300)         # the test loads sit anywhere

V_train = np.zeros((300, m))
V_test = np.zeros((300, m))

for i in range(300):
    V_train[i] = deflection(c_train[i])
    V_test[i] = deflection(c_test[i])

scale = 1/np.abs(V_train).max()                # the deflections are of order 1e-3

ct = torch.tensor(c_train.reshape(-1, 1), dtype = torch.float32)
vt = torch.tensor(V_train*scale, dtype = torch.float32)
In [ ]:
# the unconstrained network

torch.manual_seed(0)

net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 64), nn.Tanh(),
                    nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.Tanh(),
                    nn.Linear(64, m))

opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr = 0.002)

for k in range(3000):
    loss = torch.mean((net(ct) - vt)**2)

    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()

print('plain network        train loss = %.2e' % loss.item())

plain network        train loss = 8.63e-06
In [ ]:
# data augmentation: each load and its mirror, with the label mirrored as well

c_aug = np.concatenate([c_train, -c_train])
V_aug = np.vstack([V_train, V_train[:, ::-1]])

ca = torch.tensor(c_aug.reshape(-1, 1), dtype = torch.float32)
va = torch.tensor(V_aug*scale, dtype = torch.float32)

torch.manual_seed(0)

net_aug = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 64), nn.Tanh(),
                        nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.Tanh(),
                        nn.Linear(64, m))

opt = torch.optim.Adam(net_aug.parameters(), lr = 0.002)

for k in range(3000):
    loss = torch.mean((net_aug(ca) - va)**2)

    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()

print('data augmentation    train loss = %.2e' % loss.item())

data augmentation    train loss = 3.38e-06
In [ ]:
# the symmetrized model, trained as such: the optimizer never sees the raw network alone

torch.manual_seed(0)

net_sym = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 64), nn.Tanh(),
                        nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.Tanh(),
                        nn.Linear(64, m))

opt = torch.optim.Adam(net_sym.parameters(), lr = 0.002)

for k in range(3000):
    pred = 0.5*(net_sym(ct) + torch.flip(net_sym(-ct), [1]))

    loss = torch.mean((pred - vt)**2)

    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()

print('symmetrized network  train loss = %.2e' % loss.item())

symmetrized network  train loss = 1.25e-06

Two numbers are reported for each model. The equivariance error is the relative discrepancy $\lVert f(-c) - R\,f(c)\rVert / \lVert f(c)\rVert$ averaged over the test loads; it is a property of the map alone and never looks at the exact solution. The test RMSE compares the prediction with the exact deflection, and is the accuracy.

In [ ]:
def predict(network, c):
    with torch.no_grad():
        return network(torch.tensor(c.reshape(-1, 1), dtype = torch.float32)).numpy()/scale


def symmetrize(network, c):                    # 0.5*[ f(q) + R f(Rq) ]
    return 0.5*(predict(network, c) + predict(network, -c)[:, ::-1])


print('%-26s %18s %14s' % ('', 'equivariance error', 'test RMSE'))

for name, P, PR in [('plain network', predict(net, c_test), predict(net, -c_test)),
                    ('data augmentation', predict(net_aug, c_test), predict(net_aug, -c_test)),
                    ('symmetrized, trained', symmetrize(net_sym, c_test), symmetrize(net_sym, -c_test))]:
    error = np.mean(np.linalg.norm(PR - P[:, ::-1], axis = 1)/np.linalg.norm(P, axis = 1))
    print('%-26s %18.2e %14.3e' % (name, error, np.sqrt(np.mean((P - V_test)**2))))

                           equivariance error      test RMSE
plain network                        1.06e+00      1.525e-03
data augmentation                    1.09e-02      1.947e-05
symmetrized, trained                 0.00e+00      1.442e-05
In [ ]:
c_one = np.array([0.25])                       # a load on the right half, never seen in training

v_exact = deflection(c_one[0])
v_raw = predict(net, c_one)[0]
v_mirror = predict(net, -c_one)[0][::-1]
v_sym = symmetrize(net_sym, c_one)[0]

plt.figure(figsize = (12, 4))

plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
plt.plot([c_one[0], c_one[0]], [0, 1], 'k', linewidth = 2)
plt.plot([-c_one[0], -c_one[0]], [0, 1], 'k--', linewidth = 1.5)
plt.xlim(-0.5, 0.5)
plt.legend(['load at c', 'mirrored load'], fontsize = 11)
plt.grid(True)
plt.xlabel('x', fontsize = 12)
plt.ylabel('q(x)', fontsize = 12)

plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
plt.plot(x, v_exact, 'k', linewidth = 3, alpha = 0.3)
plt.plot(x, v_sym, 'b--', linewidth = 1.5)
plt.legend(['exact', 'symmetrized network'], fontsize = 11)
plt.grid(True)
plt.xlabel('x', fontsize = 12)
plt.ylabel('v(x)', fontsize = 12)

plt.show()

The unconstrained network is not equivariant by any margin — the discrepancy between the two sides of the identity is as large as the prediction itself — and on loads placed where it was never trained its error is two thirds of the deflection it is meant to produce. It learned the left half of the problem and nothing about the right.


Augmentation repairs most of that. The equivariance error falls to about one percent and the accuracy becomes good, because the mirrored copies are in effect the missing half of the training set. What it does not deliver is the identity itself: one percent is small, but it is not zero, and nothing keeps it small on a load unlike those it was shown.


The symmetrized network is exactly equivariant, to every digit printed, and it is also the most accurate, from data covering half the beam, because the construction supplies the other half before the optimizer ever sees it. The identity is not something it learned; it holds for any parameters, and training only has to make the average right.


The figure is the same statement for a single load on the right half of the beam, where no training load ever sat: the symmetrized prediction lies on the exact solution.




7. Invariance¶

Equivariance is the right requirement when the output carries direction or position. When it does not — when the output is a single number that should not change at all under the transformation — the requirement is invariance, and the constructions change in one small but decisive way.


7.1. What Invariance Means¶

7.1.1. Definition¶

A network is invariant with respect to a transformation $T$ when


$$ f(Tq) = f(q) . $$


This is the special case of equivariance in which $T$ acts trivially on the output.


A network predicting the total energy of a molecule should return the same value however the molecule is rotated or translated, because total energy is a scalar. A network classifying an image as "cat" or "not cat" should return the same label when the image is shifted a few pixels.

7.1.2. Equivariance or Invariance?¶

The distinction is decided by the output, not by the transformation.


If the output is a field or a vector — something with a direction or a position — equivariance is the requirement, and the transformation must be undone on the output. If the output is a single number with no directional content, invariance is the requirement, and there is nothing to undo.


The two symmetrization formulas differ by exactly that factor:


$$ \tilde{f}(q) = \frac{1}{2}\bigl[\, f(q) + R\,f(Rq) \,\bigr] \qquad\text{(equivariant)} , $$


$$ \tilde{f}(q) = \frac{1}{2}\bigl[\, f(q) + f(Rq) \,\bigr] \qquad\text{(invariant)} . $$


7.2. Enforcing Invariance¶

7.2.1. Invariant Input Features¶

Transform the raw input into features that are unchanged by the transformation, and pass only those to the network. For rotational invariance, pairwise distances between points serve, since distances do not change under rotation. The network then operates entirely on invariant quantities and its output is invariant automatically.


This is the strongest and most efficient of the three, because the invariance is built into the representation and costs one forward pass. It requires knowing a complete set of invariant features; an incomplete set discards information the network may need.


The figure shows the idea for two interacting particles.


A complete invariant for two particles. The positions $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ change under rotation and translation, but the distance $r_{12} = \lVert r_1 - r_2\rVert$ between them does not. A network fed $(q_1, q_2, r_{12})$ rather than the raw coordinates returns an energy $U$ that is invariant by construction.

7.2.2. Pooling over Transformations¶

Evaluate the network on all transformed versions of the input and aggregate:


$$ \tilde{f}(q) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} f(T_i q) $$


Because the sum runs over the whole group, transforming the input merely permutes the terms and the result is unchanged. A maximum can replace the average,


$$ \tilde{f}(q) = \max_{i}\, f(T_i q) , $$


with the same argument. This is exact and architecture-free, at the price of $n$ forward passes.

7.2.3. Data Augmentation¶

Train on transformed versions of each example. From a pair $(q_i, y_i)$ with a scalar label, generate


$$ (T q_i,\; y_i) . $$


Unlike the equivariant case of Section 6.2.3, the label is left unchanged, which is precisely the difference between the two requirements. The route is easy and approximate: the network is encouraged towards invariance but is not forced into it.


7.3. A Worked Case: the Strain Energy of the Same Beam¶

7.3.1. Why the Energy Is Invariant¶

Take the clamped-clamped beam of Section 6.3 again, on $x \in [-L/2,\, L/2]$ with load $q(x)$, but let the network predict the total strain energy


$$ U = \int_{-L/2}^{L/2} \frac{1}{2}\, EI \left(\frac{d^{2}v}{dx^{2}}\right)^{2} dx , $$


where $EI$ is the bending stiffness.


Flipping the load flips the deflection, by the equivariance established in Section 6.3.1 — but the energy is an integral of the squared curvature over the whole beam, and reflecting the integrand merely reverses the order in which it is integrated. The energy is therefore unchanged:


$$ U[Rq] = U[q] . $$


The deflection field is equivariant; the scalar computed from it is invariant. Both statements describe the same physics, and which one applies to a given network is settled by what that network outputs.


Accordingly, a network predicting the energy should satisfy


$$ f(Rq) = f(q) , $$


and if this is not enforced it will generally predict two different energies for $q$ and $Rq$ — two different answers to what is physically one question.

7.3.2. The Three Strategies Applied¶

Invariant input features. Symmetrize the load before it reaches the network:


$$ \tilde{q}(x) = q(x) + q(-x) . $$


Since $R\tilde{q} = \tilde{q}$, the network only ever sees symmetric inputs and its output is invariant. Note what this costs: the antisymmetric part of the load has been discarded, and it does contribute to the energy. Here the feature is invariant but not complete, which is the general hazard of this route.


Pooling over transformations. Evaluate the network on both the original and the flipped load and average:


$$ \tilde{f}(q) = \frac{1}{2}\bigl[\, f(q) + f(Rq) \,\bigr] . $$


No inverse transformation appears, because the output is a scalar. The result satisfies $\tilde{f}(Rq) = \tilde{f}(q)$ identically, whatever $f$ has learned, at the cost of two forward passes. This is the invariant counterpart of the construction of Section 6.3.2, and comparing the two formulas side by side is the clearest way to hold the distinction.


Data augmentation. Train on both $(q_i, U_i)$ and $(Rq_i, U_i)$, with the label unchanged. The network is encouraged to return the same energy for both, but may still differ slightly on unseen loads. It is the easiest to implement, requiring no change to the architecture or to inference, and the only one of the three with no exact guarantee.


7.4. Invariant Features in Practice¶

7.4.1. An Experiment¶

Two point charges in the plane interact with the Coulomb energy


$$ U = \frac{k\,q_1 q_2}{r_{12}} , \qquad r_{12} = \lVert r_1 - r_2 \rVert , $$


which depends on the separation alone and not on where the pair sits or how it is turned. Two networks are trained on the same energies: one reads the four raw coordinates, the other reads only $r_{12}$. To make the difference visible, the training configurations are restricted to a quarter turn of orientation, while the test configurations use every orientation.

In [ ]:
k = 1.0
q1 = 1.0
q2 = -1.0

m = 2000

# training pairs: the orientation covers a quarter turn only

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

r_train = rng.uniform(0.5, 2.0, m)                          # separation
th = rng.uniform(0, np.pi/4, m)                             # orientation
c = rng.uniform(-1, 1, (m, 2))                              # centre of the pair

d = 0.5*np.stack([r_train*np.cos(th), r_train*np.sin(th)], axis = 1)

X_train = np.hstack([c + d, c - d])                         # the four raw coordinates
U_train = k*q1*q2/r_train

# test pairs: every orientation

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

r_test = rng.uniform(0.5, 2.0, m)
th = rng.uniform(0, 2*np.pi, m)
c = rng.uniform(-1, 1, (m, 2))

d = 0.5*np.stack([r_test*np.cos(th), r_test*np.sin(th)], axis = 1)

X_test = np.hstack([c + d, c - d])
U_test = k*q1*q2/r_test
In [ ]:
# the network that reads the four raw coordinates

torch.manual_seed(0)

net_raw = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4, 40), nn.Tanh(),
                       nn.Linear(40, 40), nn.Tanh(),
                       nn.Linear(40, 1))

a = torch.tensor(X_train, dtype = torch.float32)
b = torch.tensor(U_train, dtype = torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)

opt = torch.optim.Adam(net_raw.parameters(), lr = 0.005)

for i in range(4000):
    loss = torch.mean((net_raw(a) - b)**2)

    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()

p_train_raw = net_raw(a).detach().numpy().ravel()
p_test_raw = net_raw(torch.tensor(X_test, dtype = torch.float32)).detach().numpy().ravel()
In [ ]:
# the network that reads the separation only

torch.manual_seed(0)

net_inv = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 40), nn.Tanh(),
                       nn.Linear(40, 40), nn.Tanh(),
                       nn.Linear(40, 1))

a = torch.tensor(r_train.reshape(-1, 1), dtype = torch.float32)
b = torch.tensor(U_train, dtype = torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)

opt = torch.optim.Adam(net_inv.parameters(), lr = 0.005)

for i in range(4000):
    loss = torch.mean((net_inv(a) - b)**2)

    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()

p_train_inv = net_inv(a).detach().numpy().ravel()
p_test_inv = net_inv(torch.tensor(r_test.reshape(-1, 1), dtype = torch.float32)).detach().numpy().ravel()
In [ ]:
print('%-20s %10s   %s' % ('', 'train RMSE', 'test RMSE (all orientations)'))
print('%-20s %10.4f   %10.4f'
      % ('raw coordinates', np.sqrt(np.mean((p_train_raw - U_train)**2)),
         np.sqrt(np.mean((p_test_raw - U_test)**2))))
print('%-20s %10.4f   %10.4f'
      % ('distance r12 only', np.sqrt(np.mean((p_train_inv - U_train)**2)),
         np.sqrt(np.mean((p_test_inv - U_test)**2))))

                     train RMSE   test RMSE (all orientations)
raw coordinates          0.0053       1.3732
distance r12 only        0.0008       0.0007

The aggregate numbers already tell the story, but the direct test is better: take one configuration, rotate it through a full turn without changing the separation, and watch the prediction.

In [ ]:
r0 = 1.2
angles = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 73)
pred_raw = np.zeros(73)

for i in range(73):                            # the same pair, turned through a full circle
    dx1 = 0.5*r0*np.cos(angles[i])
    dy1 = 0.5*r0*np.sin(angles[i])

    pair = np.array([[dx1, dy1, -dx1, -dy1]])
    pred_raw[i] = net_raw(torch.tensor(pair, dtype = torch.float32)).detach().item()

pred_inv = net_inv(torch.tensor([[r0]], dtype = torch.float32)).detach().item()

print('one configuration at r = %.1f, rotated through a full turn' % r0)
print('   exact energy                       %+.4f' % (k*q1*q2/r0))
print('   raw-coordinate network : min %+.4f   max %+.4f   spread %.4f'
      % (pred_raw.min(), pred_raw.max(), pred_raw.max() - pred_raw.min()))
print('   distance-only network  :     %+.4f   (constant, the input never changes)' % pred_inv)

one configuration at r = 1.2, rotated through a full turn
   exact energy                       -0.8333
   raw-coordinate network : min -3.1757   max -0.8284   spread 2.3473
   distance-only network  :     -0.8328   (constant, the input never changes)
In [ ]:
plt.figure(figsize = (6, 4))
plt.plot(angles, pred_raw, 'r--', linewidth = 1.5)
plt.plot(angles, pred_inv*np.ones(73), 'b--', linewidth = 1.5)
plt.plot(angles, (k*q1*q2/r0)*np.ones(73), 'k', linewidth = 4, alpha = 0.3)
plt.legend(['raw coordinates', 'distance only', 'exact'], fontsize = 12)
plt.grid(True)
plt.xlabel('orientation of the pair', fontsize = 12)
plt.ylabel('predicted energy', fontsize = 12)
plt.show()

The network given the raw coordinates fits its training set closely and then fails on the test set by orders of magnitude more, and its prediction for one physical configuration swings widely as that configuration is merely turned around. The network given $r_{12}$ has the same accuracy on both sets, and its prediction is exactly constant under rotation, its flat line lying on top of the exact one in the figure, because the number it receives does not change. The invariance was not learned; it was made unnecessary to learn.




Summary¶

Key takeaways


| Constraint | Hard enforcement | Soft enforcement | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | $f \geq 0$ | $\hat{f} = \exp(v)$ or $\log(1 + e^{v})$ | $\bigl[\max(0, -f)\bigr]^2$ | | $f \leq 0$ | $\hat{f} = -\exp(v)$ | $\bigl[\max(0, f)\bigr]^2$ | | monotone increasing | $f(x_0) + \int_{x_0}^{x}\exp(g)\,dt$; non-negative weights | $\bigl[\max(0, f(x_1) - f(x_2))\bigr]^2$ | | $v = g$ on $\partial\Omega$ | $\hat{v} = g + s\,v$, $\;s|_{\partial\Omega} = 0$ | $\bigl(\hat{v} - g\bigr)^2$ on sampled boundary points | | $v(x,0) = v_0$ | $\hat{v} = v_0 + \tau(t)\,v$, $\;\tau(0) = 0$ | $\bigl(\hat{v}(\cdot,0) - v_0\bigr)^2$ | | $\int_\Omega v = C$ | $\hat{v} = v + \bigl(C - \int_\Omega v\bigr)/|\Omega|$ | $\bigl(\int_\Omega v - C\bigr)^2$ | | $v > 0$ and $\int_\Omega v = 1$ | continuous softmax | both penalties | | equivariance | group layers; $\tfrac12[f(q) + R f(Rq)]$ | augmentation with transformed labels | | invariance | invariant features; $\tfrac12[f(q) + f(Rq)]$ | augmentation with unchanged labels |


  • A soft constraint is a term in the loss; a hard constraint is a property of the architecture. The first applies to anything differentiable and is satisfied approximately; the second is exact for every parameter value but exists only where an encoding is known. Raising the penalty weight does not turn one into the other — it only stiffens the optimization.
  • The recipe behind every hard constraint is the same. Identify what must hold exactly, write a form in which it holds identically, and let the network occupy the freedom that remains: $\exp(v)$ for a sign, $g + s\,v$ for a boundary value, an additive shift for an integral, a group average for a symmetry.
  • Sign and bound constraints are essentially free. A smooth surjection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto the admissible set, composed with the network, costs one elementwise evaluation and removes a penalty weight from the objective.
  • Monotonicity is a statement about the derivative, so the exact constructions either model the derivative and integrate it, or restrict the weights so that the composition cannot decrease. The second is simpler and strictly less expressive.
  • Boundary and initial conditions are the clearest case for hard enforcement: they are known exactly, they hold from initialization onwards, and they can never be traded against the equation residual during training. As penalties they compete with the equation, need two weights that are hard to balance, and leave an error at the edge that an elliptic problem carries into the whole interior.
  • Equivariance means $f(Tq) = T f(q)$, with the transformation acting on the input on one side and on the output on the other. Averaging over a group with the transformation undone on the output, $\tilde{f}(q) = \tfrac12\bigl[f(q) + R f(Rq)\bigr]$ for a reflection, is exactly equivariant for any network, at the price of one extra forward pass.
  • Invariance means $f(Tq) = f(q)$, and its symmetrization is the same formula with the output transformation removed. Which of the two is wanted is decided by the output: a field or a vector calls for equivariance, a scalar for invariance.
  • The symmetry of a particular solution is a consequence, not the requirement. A symmetric load is a fixed point of $R$, so $R\tilde{f}(q) = \tilde{f}(Rq) = \tilde{f}(q)$ and the predicted deflection is even. Building only for that case would leave every asymmetric load unconstrained.

  • The constructions cost little and the measurements say so. In the experiments of this notebook the constrained model matched the unconstrained one on training loss and on error against the truth, while removing every violation: the softplus network never went negative where the plain one did over part of the extrapolation range; the monotone network decreased nowhere where the plain one decreased at twelve intervals; the masked network was exactly zero at both ends, where the plain network's largest error was at those ends. A correct prior is not a restriction that has to be paid for.
  • An exact construction is exact for a reason that can be checked. Commuting with the reflection to machine precision, returning zero at a masked boundary, integrating to the prescribed constant — each is one line of verification, and each fails loudly when the construction is subtly wrong.

Looking ahead. Every construction in this notebook fixes what the network cannot get wrong; none of them says anything about what it should get right in between. That is the work of the training objective, and the two meet in physics-informed learning, where the governing equation itself becomes the loss and the constructions above decide which of its conditions are paid for by a penalty weight and which are imposed for free. The same distinction reappears at the level of the architecture in operator learning, where a translation-equivariant spectral layer is chosen for exactly the reason given in Section 6.2.1 — a symmetry that is built in is a symmetry that never has to be learned from data.
